entries.description:
Rows and columns held in memory — a table of values. The columns come first: each has a name and a type (Columns.AddColumn). Rows are added with Add and are the table's OWN rows: `row.Amount = 10` changes the table, and a row taken out of it by Find, FindRows or an index is the same row, not a copy. A table is walked with Foreach in row order and read by index, `Table[0]`.

A LINQ query answers with a table (`from o in orders select { Item = o.Item, Amount = o.Amount }`), so the result of a query is read exactly like one made by hand. Ordering by several keys, filtering and grouping are the query's to say — `orderby o.Item, o.Amount descending` — not arguments of the table's own methods.

The table's columns. AddColumn declares one, RemoveColumn takes one away, Find answers with one by its name or Undefined, Count says how many there are; `Table.Columns[i]` is a column's description, with Name, Types, Caption, Width and Indexing.

Indexing = True on a column that Find and FindRows search by makes them answer through an index built on first use and rebuilt when the rows change, instead of reading every row.
entries.example:
Table.Columns.AddColumn("Code", New TypeDescription("String"));
Table.Columns[0].Indexing = True;   // Find / FindRows by Code use an index

entries.signature: Columns.AddColumn(name : string, type : TypeDescription | Type = any, caption : string = name, width : number = 80)
entries.description: Declares a column and answers with its description. The TYPE decides what the column holds and how its cells compare, sort and total. A column added WITHOUT a type — or with Undefined for one — is of any type: each cell keeps exactly what was written, so after `AddColumn("N")` the line `Row.N = 5` holds the number 5 and `Row.N = "5"` the string. Pass a type when the column must hold one kind: `New TypeDescription("Number")`, or `New TypeDescription("Number", New QualifierNumber(15, 2))` to keep two digits after the point. A type named without a qualifier limits nothing: a string of any length, a date with its time. A Type value is taken as well as a TypeDescription; anything else raises.
entries.parameters:
name — the column's name, as rows read it (`Row.<name>`).
type — a TypeDescription or a Type; left out or Undefined, the column takes any value.
caption — the header shown in a form; left out, the name.
width — the width in a form; left out, 80.
entries.return_descr: The column's description (Name, Types, Caption, Width, Indexing).

entries.description: Takes a column away, with its values in every row. A name the table does not have is left alone.
Answers with the column of that name, or Undefined when the table has none: whether a column is there is asked without reading it. The name is compared regardless of case, as a row's field is read.
entries.return_descr: The column's description (Name, Types, Caption, Width, Indexing), or Undefined.
entries.example: Column = Table.Columns.Find("Discount");   // Undefined when the table has no such column

entries.description: The number of columns the table has.

A row of a table: one field per column, read and written by the column's name. A row belongs to its table — writing a field writes the table, and the same row reached twice (by index, by Find, from FindRows) is the same row. A value written into a field is kept as the column's type says.
entries.example:
Row = Table.Find("Paper", "Item");
Row.Amount = Row.Amount + 1;   // the table's row is changed

entries.description: Adds a row at the end and answers with it, every field empty for its column's type.
How many rows the table has. The last row is `Table[Table.Count() - 1]`; an index past it raises.
Removes a row — given as the row itself or by its index. The rows after it move up by one.
entries.parameters: row — a row of this table, or its index from 0.

entries.description: Removes every row. The columns stay.
The first row, in row order, whose field in `column` equals `value` — or Undefined when there is none. On a column with Indexing = True it answers through the column's index.
entries.parameters:
value — what the field must equal.
column — the column's name.
entries.example: Row = Table.Find("Paper", "Item");   // Undefined when no row has it

entries.description: Every row whose fields equal the filter's values — `column = value` for each key of the Structure, all of them at once — in row order. The rows are the table's own. An empty filter answers with every row; a key that names no column raises rather than finding nothing. When a column in the filter has Indexing = True, its index picks the candidates.
entries.syntax_block: Rows = Table.FindRows(New Structure("Warehouse, Item", Warehouse, Item));
entries.parameters: filter — a Structure of column = value.

entries.description: The sum of a column, added exactly — 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.3. An empty field adds nothing and an empty table totals 0. A column that is not there raises, and so does a field that holds something other than a number, naming its row: a wrong total that looks right is the worst answer a sum can give. A column that is to be totalled is best declared as a Number, so a string cannot get into it.

Puts the rows in the order of ONE column — the rows themselves move, so the table then IS in that order. Rows with equal values keep the order they had. A column that is not there raises and nothing moves.

An order over several columns, each its own way, is a query's to say: `from r in Table orderby r.Priority, r.Level descending select r`.
entries.parameters:
column — the column's name.
ascending — True (the default) for ascending, False for descending.

entries.description: The values of one column, in row order, as an Array — the way to ask for plain values when a table is what came back. A column that is not there gives an empty Array.

A new table with the same columns — name, type, caption, width and indexing — and the same rows. Nothing is shared: a row changed or a column added in the copy leaves the original as it was. The values in the cells are copied as values, so an object or a reference a cell holds is the same one in both tables.
entries.example:
Totals = Sales.Clone();
Totals.GroupBy("Item", "Amount");   // Sales keeps its rows

entries.description: Where the row stands in the table, from 0. A row of another table — a clone's included — or anything that is not a row answers -1.
entries.parameters: row — a row of a table.

entries.description:
Folds the table IN PLACE: the rows that hold equal values in every group column become one row, each sum column holds the total of the rows it stands for, and every other column is removed. Both lists are column names separated by commas; blanks around a name are ignored. The groups keep the order in which their first row stood. A sum cell that is not a number adds nothing.

A name that is not a column raises before anything changes, and so does a column named in both lists. To keep the original rows, Clone the table first.
entries.parameters:
groupColumns — the columns whose values make a group.
sumColumns — the columns to total; left out, only the group columns remain.
entries.example: Sales.GroupBy("Item", "Amount");   // one row per item, its amount totalled

entries.description: Writes one value into the listed columns of every row; with no list, into every column. The list is column names separated by commas. A name that is not a column raises before any cell is written.
entries.parameters:
value — what every cell gets.
columns — the columns to fill, separated by commas; left out or empty, all of them.

entries.description: A row of a table — what Add, Find, FindRows, an index and Foreach hand out. Its fields are the table's columns, read and written by name; the row belongs to its table (see Row). Two rows are equal (`=`) when they are the same row of the same table, and Index says where one stands. Rows are made by the table's Add, never with New.

The column collection of a table — what Table.Columns answers: Count, Find, AddColumn and RemoveColumn (see Columns). `Columns[i]` is a column by its index from 0, and an index past the last column raises; Foreach walks the columns in order.

One column's description — what AddColumn, Find and `Columns[i]` answer: Name, Types (a TypeDescription), Caption, Width (80 unless given) and Indexing. Only Indexing can be written; a value written into the others is ignored and the column stays as it was. A column's name and type are the ones it was added with — to change them, remove the column and add it again.
